What this adds to the program

  • The valuation toolkit, from the channel's own interview series. The repo builds a DCF from scratch (unit 06 whats a business worth) but has no WACC, CAPM or beta anywhere. New here: the channel's worked cost of debt (7% × 0.75 = 5.25%) and cost of equity (4.25% + 1.25 × 5.5% = 11.125%), the theory-vs-practice split on beta (forward Barra vs. Bloomberg adjusted, and why the sell side standardizes for litigation), the U-shaped answer to "how does debt change WACC," and the earnings-yield vs. cost-of-equity confusion that conflates EPS accretion with valuation.
  • Enterprise value has no home in the repo. GLOSSARY.md and learn/unit-06 teach DCF as "discount the cash" but never separate equity value from firm value. The channel's X/xAI short is the cleanest demonstration available: a "$33B" deal and a "$44B" deal that are the same price. This note adds EV, and why every LBO/M&A headline must be decoded through it.
  • The LBO is in the repo only as a house analogy (tiger sisters private capital 101, Toys "R" Us). New here: Kristen's worked LBO ($3M equity → $9M, 3.0x, ~25% IRR, decomposed into EBITDA growth vs. debt paydown), the equity check as the real risk dial (TXU ~18% vs. EA ~65%), sources & uses, cash-free/debt-free and rollover equity (Skechers), and who actually funds the debt.
  • How finance people are paid, with numbers. trading floor mechanics says entry pay is "roughly six figures" and stops. New here: the base/bonus split by level (IB vs. PE/private credit), the one-third cash / one-third deferred cash / one-third deferred stock structure, why deferral makes seniors expensive to poach, how the EU bonus cap raised fixed pay, and carry economics by fund size. This is applied agency theory (canon jensen meckling agency theory).
  • Failure modes and firm models: First Brands (double-pledged receivables), the "11,000-to-1" Treasury short, JPMorgan's $20B sole underwrite, 2008's bilateral-swap contagion; the IPO pop as a transfer to allocated investors (Figma ≈ $3B); and Scott Bok on why advice-only boutiques exist and why he sold Greenhill into Mizuho anyway.

4 · Concepts

4.1 The three-statement model, and when you don't need one

  • What it is: A linked projection of a company's income statement, cash flow statement and balance sheet in Excel, so that one assumption change (say, revenue growth) flows through profit, cash and the balance sheet at once. It is the "language" Kristen says bankers speak; the DCF, the LBO and the merger model are all built on top of its outputs.
  • How it works (Kristen, ESSENTIALS for Building a 3 Statement Financial Model): She orders the statements income statement → cash flow statement → balance sheet, not the textbook IS → BS → CFS, because that is the path one dollar takes: net income closes the income statement and opens the cash flow statement (the indirect method); the cash flow statement converts it to a change in cash; that cash lands on the balance sheet. Her build sequence: 1. Income statement from sales down to net income, leaving holes for interest expense and interest income (they need the debt and cash balances, which don't exist yet) and for D&A (needs capex). 2. Balance sheet line by line through supporting schedules (working capital, PP&E, debt), top to bottom, with cash left for last. 3. Every balance sheet projection has a twin on the cash flow statement (more PP&E is capex; more receivables is a cash outflow). "You can't do one without the other": if a line moves on one statement and not the other, the model won't balance, and you lose hours finding it. Once the schedules exist the holes fill and the model closes (interest depends on cash, which depends on interest: the circularity analysts switch on iterative calculation for, which the hosts don't name).
  • Business significance: A DCF does not need the full linked model: it uses only unlevered cash flows, so you can pull EBITDA, D&A, capex and the change in working capital into an output tab and skip the debt and the balance sheet. Some LBOs on the sponsors desk were run on cash flows plus a debt schedule only. But a PE modeling test will expect the full three statements. And her teaching observation: students say two days building one taught them more accounting than a semester of class.
  • Forces & impact (the Financial Modeling & Excel MUST KNOWS episode): Banking models are valued because they are a transferable representation of a business, unlike trading-desk models (convertible pricing with Monte Carlo engines, CDO models) that programmers build, nobody formats because no client sees them, and whose skill doesn't travel. Conventions are near-universal: blue inputs, black formulas, green links to other sheets. Keyboard over mouse because a model is thousands of formulas; Windows over Mac Excel; learn native shortcuts for interviews (you won't have your add-ins on someone else's machine), then load productivity add-ins on the job. Excel inertia is structural: Morgan Stanley was still on Excel 2003 in 2010 because the ribbon broke everyone's key sequences. The model's output is a conversation with a CEO, not a P&L position, so presentation is part of the substance.
  • With vs. without: With linked statements, every assumption is forced to be internally consistent (growth needs working capital and capex, which need funding). Without them, a cash-flow-only model can assume growth for free; the balance sheet is the check that catches it.
  • Applies when you need debt capacity, credit stats, or EPS (LBO, merger, restructuring). Breaks when it's overkill: a quick DCF or a screening valuation.
  • Channel example: ESSENTIALS for Building a 3 Statement Financial Model; Financial Modeling & Excel MUST KNOWS for Investment Banking x Macabacus (with Macabacus founder Ryan McGregor, ex-Lehman, who built the tool in 2008 after being laid off; acquired by CFI in 2021).
  • Counterpoint: The modeling episode is partly an ad (Macabacus is a sponsor; the hosts were launching their own modeling course). The craft claims hold, but "you can knock out a model in 20 minutes to an hour" is Kristen-speed, not analyst-speed.
  • Links: unit 02 cash vs profit (why net income isn't cash); unit 03 what a company owns and owes (the balance sheet); aapl 10k fy2025 (a real set of statements to model).

4.2 Equity value vs. enterprise value

  • What it is: Equity value is what the shares are worth. Enterprise value (EV) is what the whole operating business is worth: equity plus debt (strictly, plus debt and preferred, minus cash). Buying a company means buying the equity and taking on its debt, so EV is the real price.
  • How it works: The hosts' house analogy (#1 Top 5 Technical Questions): a $5M house bought with $1M down and a $4M mortgage. You didn't buy a $1M house; you bought a $5M one, financed 20/80. The X/xAI short applies it: xAI bought X in an all-stock deal at $33B equity value, but X carried ~$12B of debt (mostly from Musk's 2022 buyout), so EV ≈ $45B. In 2022 Musk paid $44B when X had ~$0.6B of debt, EV ≈ $44.6B. Arithmetic: 33 + 12 = 45 vs. 44 + 0.6 = 44.6. Same price; the "markdown" was a financing change, not a valuation change.
  • Business significance: Every multiple that matters to a buyer (EV/EBITDA, the LBO's 20x for EA) is EV-based, because EBITDA is earned for all capital providers. Equity multiples (P/E) belong to shareholders only. Mixing them is the commonest error in deal headlines, and the hosts note that TXU is reported as both a "$30B" and a "$45B" LBO for exactly this reason.
  • Forces & impact: Leverage moves value between the two lines. Pile on debt and, for the same EV, equity shrinks; this is the whole engine of §4.7. Second-order: a falling "valuation" can be pure re-leveraging, and a rising one can be debt paydown.
  • With vs. without: Without EV, a company with $40B of debt and $5B of market cap looks "cheap" next to a debt-free $20B one. With it you see the first costs $45B.
  • Applies when comparing businesses with different capital structures, or acquisitions. Breaks when "debt" is ambiguous: leases, pensions, off-balance-sheet obligations (First Brands, §4.12), minority interests. EV is only as honest as the debt list.
  • Channel example: The Truth About the $33Bn Elon Musk's xAI Paid for X; #1 of Top 5 Technical Questions.
  • Counterpoint: The short says "true value is EV." Value to whom matters: xAI's outside shareholders paid in stock, so their question is the relative value of two private stocks, both marked by a party on both sides (§4.16). EV arithmetic doesn't fix a soft mark.
  • Links: unit 06 whats a business worth (cash-flow logic this sits on); GLOSSARY "Leverage".

4.3 The DCF: intrinsic value, and the interview answer

  • What it is: One of the three standard ways to value a company, alongside public comparables (what similar listed companies trade at) and precedent transactions (what similar companies were bought for). The discounted cash flow analysis is the intrinsic one: value comes from the cash this business will produce, not from what other businesses fetch.
  • How it works (Kristen, Walk Me Through the DCF in Under 3 Minutes): Three steps. 1. Project unlevered free cash flow (cash generated for all capital providers, before interest) for 5, 10 or 15 years. Academically you project until the company reaches steady state; in practice you stop at 5–15. 2. Add a terminal value for everything after the projection: either the perpetuity growth method (grow the last year's cash flow forever at a constant rate) or the exit multiple method (assume the business is sold at a multiple, usually of EBITDA). Academics dislike the second, she notes; banks use it routinely. 3. Discount every cash flow and the terminal value back at the WACC (§4.4) and add them up. The sum is enterprise value (§4.2), not equity value. Why discount (DCF in Investment Banking: Theory vs. Reality): inflation, the risk the cash never arrives, and opportunity cost (money today could sit in a ~5% Treasury). Kristen's point on effort: she could explain the DCF in one three-minute video; the WACC took three.
  • Business significance: The DCF is the methodology that answers "what is this worth to anyone," which is why it anchors fairness opinions and buy-side underwriting. For a banker it is one bar on the football field next to comps and precedents; the episode on modeling stresses it's part of a holistic picture shown to a CEO, not a trading model.
  • Forces & impact: Rates move the discount rate; the terminal value usually carries most of the value, so the exit multiple quietly imports market pricing back into an "intrinsic" method. The hosts' recurring Industry joke makes the second-order point: lower the WACC and the valuation goes up, so a DCF can be tuned toward the answer the client wants to hear (§4.4 on why banks standardize inputs).
  • With vs. without: With a DCF, a buyer has a value independent of a frothy comp set. Without it, every valuation is relative, and a sector-wide bubble looks "fairly priced" against itself.
  • Applies when cash flows are forecastable (mature, positive FCF). Breaks when the terminal value is most of the answer, cash flows are negative for years (early-stage), or the exit multiple method turns it back into a comps analysis.
  • Channel example: Walk Me Through the DCF in Under 3 Minutes; DCF in Investment Banking: Theory vs. Reality.
  • Counterpoint: The three-minute answer is an interview script; it doesn't say how sensitive the output is. A 1-point change in WACC or terminal growth can move value 15–25% on a typical model, which is why the football field shows ranges, not points (standard practice, not stated by the hosts).
  • Links: unit 06 whats a business worth (the repo's DCF built from scratch); bloomberg terminal instrumentation (XLTP DCF template).

4.4 The WACC: cost of debt, cost of equity, and choosing a beta

  • What it is: The weighted average cost of capital is the DCF's discount rate: the blended return that lenders and shareholders require, weighted by how much of the business each funds. WACC = %debt × after-tax cost of debt + %equity × cost of equity.
  • How it works (the channel's three-part WACC series plus the beta segment of Theory vs. Reality):
  • Cost of debt. Use what the company would pay to borrow today: the yield to maturity on its long-dated bonds, not the coupon. A bond issued in 2020 with a 3% coupon may now yield 7%, because its price fell when rates rose. Interest is tax-deductible, so multiply by (1 − t). Tax rate: 21% US federal plus 1–5% state and local, so ~25% is the standard assumption (use local rates for a foreign company). 7% × (1 − 25%) = 5.25%.
  • Cost of equity isn't observable, so banks use CAPM: risk-free rate + levered beta × market risk premium. Risk-free = 10- or 20-year Treasury yield (for euro cash flows, the safest euro sovereign: the German Bund). Beta = how much the stock moves per 1% move in the market (β 1.25 → +1.25% when the S&P rises 1%). Market risk premium comes from the Duff & Phelps (now Kroll) valuation handbook, typically 3–7%, or from NYU's Aswath Damodaran, who publishes his free. Channel numbers: 4.25% + 1.25 × 5.5% = 11.125%.
  • Weighting (illustration, not the channel's): at 30% debt / 70% equity, 0.3 × 5.25% + 0.7 × 11.125% = 1.58% + 7.79% ≈ 9.4%. The series ends with Kristen's joke that after all this the MD says the rate looks high and to use equity research's number.
  • Which beta (Theory vs. Reality). Academics say use a forward-looking (predicted) beta, because you are discounting future cash flows; Barra publishes them, but they are a black box. Sell-side bankers mostly use historical beta from Bloomberg's BETA screen: two years of weekly returns regressed against the S&P; the slope is raw beta, and R² says how much of the stock's movement the market explains. Most banks then use adjusted beta = ⅔ × raw + ⅓ × 1.0 (Blume's observation that betas drift toward 1). Low R², a short trading history, or a private company → use peers: unlever each peer's beta to an asset beta (stripping out their leverage), take the mean or median, relever at your company's capital structure. (The standard formula, which the hosts reference but don't state: βL = βU × [1 + (1 − t) × D/E].)
  • Business significance: The WACC is where judgment hides inside a "mechanical" valuation. The sell side standardizes inputs for liability reasons: a bank writing a fairness opinion may have to defend its beta under oath, and Kristen cites a figure that 75% of acquisitions end in lawsuits. The buy side, not defending anything in court, can use R² and judgment to pick the beta that best describes the business. Same formula, different incentives.
  • Forces & impact: Rates feed in twice (risk-free rate and cost of debt), so a rising-rate environment lowers every DCF value even if the business is unchanged. Tax policy feeds the debt leg (§4.6). Bloomberg access itself is a barrier: the hosts put a terminal at ~$28k a year.
  • With vs. without: With a defensible WACC, two banks valuing the same company land in a similar range. Without standard inputs, the discount rate becomes the dial that delivers the client's number.
  • Applies when the company's risk resembles its history or its peers'. Breaks when the capital structure is about to change (an LBO: the historical beta describes a different company), or when peers aren't really peers.
  • Channel example: Breaking Down the Cost of Equity in the WACC for a DCF; #1 Top Technical Finance Concept…WACC Part 3 (cost of debt); DCF in Investment Banking: Theory vs. Reality. Part 1 (the weighting) has no transcript.
  • Counterpoint / check: The 75% lawsuit figure fits public-company deals in the 2010s merger litigation wave, not acquisitions generally. The 3–7% MRP range is wide enough that the "source" barely constrains you: 3% vs. 7% on β 1.25 is a 5-point swing in cost of equity. And a 25% tax rate in the cost of debt assumes the interest is fully deductible, which §4.6's cap can deny.
  • Links: bloomberg terminal instrumentation (BETA returns the regression, not just a number; why not to take the terminal's WACC); unit 06 whats a business worth.

4.5 Capital structure: how adding debt changes the WACC

  • What it is: The interview question "How does increasing debt impact the WACC?" The channel's answer: debt is cheaper than equity, so adding it lowers the WACC (and raises value) up to a point, after which rising default risk makes both debt and equity more expensive and the WACC rises.
  • How it works (Kristen, How Does Increasing Debt Impact the WACC):
  • Why debt is cheaper. Lenders are paid before shareholders and stand first in bankruptcy. She cites Fitch data: average recovery ~76% for first-lien loans, ~40% for bonds; equity in Bed Bath & Beyond was essentially wiped out. Lower risk, lower required return, plus the tax deduction.
  • The deduction has limits since the 2017 tax law (§4.6).
  • Three theories. Trade-off/traditional: an optimal mix exists. Pecking order: fund from retained earnings first, then debt, then new equity as a last resort, because issuing stock signals management thinks it's overvalued (she saw this on the converts desk). Modigliani–Miller: with no taxes, more debt raises the cost of equity exactly enough that value can't change; with taxes, debt adds value through the tax shield, which she reframes as a transfer from taxpayers to the company, not value creation.
  • What MM leaves out: bankruptcy costs; issuance costs (IPO fees ~6–7% vs. 12–40bp on Meta's 2023 bond deal, per the underwriting discount she looked up); the discipline debt imposes; and the fact that borrowing costs rise in steps at rating thresholds, not smoothly.
  • The converts-desk chart. For CFOs she drew cost of capital (y) against the stock's expected five-year CAGR (x). Debt is a flat line: its cost doesn't depend on the share price. Equity is a 45° line: if your stock compounds 20% a year, that is what selling stock cost you. A convertible is debt below some growth rate and equity issued at a premium above it. Moral: if you expect your stock to do badly, issue equity; if you expect it to soar, issue debt, which is exactly the signal the pecking order says investors read.
  • The commenter's error. A viewer argued cost of equity is now below cost of debt for investment-grade firms, using earnings ÷ price. That's the earnings yield (1/PE), not a cost of equity: it ignores growth and payout. It is a legitimate accretion/dilution tool: at PE 20 the earnings yield is 5%, below a 5.25% after-tax cost of debt, so funding a deal with stock dilutes EPS less than funding it with debt. EPS is an accounting, equity-only metric; WACC is a valuation input.
  • Business significance: Capital structure is a CFO's main financial lever and the whole premise of the LBO (§4.7). The EPS-vs-WACC confusion is common in boardrooms too: a deal can be accretive and still destroy value.
  • Forces & impact: Tax rates and the interest cap set the size of the shield; rates and spreads set the cost of debt; the stock's valuation sets the attractiveness of equity (a high PE makes stock cheap currency for acquisitions, §4.22 on AOL/Time Warner).
  • With vs. without: With a tax shield, leverage is subsidized and companies carry more debt than MM alone predicts. Without it (pure MM), financing is irrelevant and only operations create value.
  • Applies when the firm has taxable profits to shield and stable cash flow. Breaks when distress costs bite: past the optimum, each turn of leverage adds more expected bankruptcy cost than shield.
  • Channel example: CRITICAL Investment Banking Interview Question: How Does Increasing Debt Impact the WACC.
  • Counterpoint / corrections: Kristen says Modigliani and Miller won the Nobel together in 1985; Modigliani won in 1985, Miller in 1990. She describes the 30%-of-EBITDA cap as running 2018–2021 with EBIT from 2022, while the channel's interest-deductibility short says 2018–2022 and 2023; the statute switched to EBIT for tax years beginning in 2022. Her worked number is also off: 30% of a $150 EBITDA is $45, not $50. The "debt is cheaper" line is right on a required-return basis but says nothing about total cost once distress risk is priced into equity.
  • Links: canon jensen meckling agency theory (debt as discipline on managers); wss capital markets ma (converts, accretion/dilution in live deals).

4.6 EBIT vs. EBITDA, and the interest-deductibility cap

  • What it is: EBIT is operating profit. EBITDA adds back depreciation and amortization (D&A), non-cash charges, so it approximates operating cash flow and is always ≥ EBIT. US tax law (since 2017) caps how much interest a company may deduct at 30% of a profit measure, and which measure it is matters a lot to anyone running a leveraged balance sheet.
  • How it works (the short's numbers): EBIT $100, D&A $50, so EBITDA $150; interest expense $100.
  • Pre-2018: deduct all $100 → taxable income $0.
  • EBITDA era (cap = 30% × EBITDA = $45): taxable = 100 − 45 = $55.
  • EBIT era (cap = 30% × EBIT = $30): taxable = 100 − 30 = $70. The channel dates the switch two ways: the short says 2018–2022 then 2023; Kristen's WACC video says 2018–2021 then 2022. The statute moved to EBIT for tax years beginning in 2022; the video is right. Same company, same debt, taxable income up 27% from a definitional change, while rates were rising so interest bills grew too. PE lobbied to restore D&A; the short cites a Treasury estimate of roughly $180B of added deficit over ten years.
  • Business significance: The tax shield on interest is one of the reasons debt is "cheaper" than equity in the WACC (after-tax cost of debt = rate × (1 − t); the channel's 7% × 0.75 = 5.25%, §4.4). Cap the deduction and the effective cost of debt rises, the optimal leverage falls, and LBO returns fall. The cap hits capital-intensive, high-D&A businesses hardest under the EBIT version.
  • Forces & impact: Tax policy and rates compound: higher coupons × lower cap = shrinking shield. The companion short (Real Reason AI Companies are Rushing to Raise) makes the mirror-image point on the asset side: 100% immediate expensing of capex pulls spending forward while the rule lasts.
  • With vs. without: With an unlimited deduction, the tax code subsidizes leverage, and the marginal LBO is partly a tax trade. With a tight cap, deals must earn their return operationally.
  • Applies when the borrower's interest exceeds the cap (high-leverage, high-rate). Breaks when the company has little taxable income anyway (losses, NOLs): the cap then costs nothing today.
  • Channel example: Private Equity LBO Modeling Basics: Changes to Interest Deductibility Rules; How Does Increasing Debt Impact the WACC (same mechanics, 150/100 example).
  • Counterpoint / dated: The short was recorded while the restoration was still being lobbied. The 2025 tax law (OBBBA) restored the EBITDA-based cap and 100% bonus depreciation — verify the current Section 163(j) text before using either figure. The short also frames this as PE's issue; the cap binds any leveraged company, including utilities and telecoms.
  • Links: GLOSSARY "Leverage"; §4.4–4.5 (where the shield enters the WACC).

4.7 The LBO and the equity check

  • What it is: A leveraged buyout buys a company with a small slice of sponsor equity and a large slice of debt that the target's own cash flow must service. The equity check (equity ÷ total price) is the dial: it decides how much the sponsor's return is magnified and how much room there is before lenders lose money.
  • How it works. The channel's definition (LBO in Under 3 Minutes): buying a company financed mostly with debt, like buying an investment house with a mortgage, renovating it, and selling it. The sponsor raises value by growing sales and cutting costs, which lifts EBITDA; the company's cash flow pays down debt meanwhile; the sponsor cares about return on its own cash, not the rise in the house's price (worked numbers in §4.8). The live-deal version (hosts' figures, Eerie Similarities…EA and 2007 TXU):
TXU (2007) Electronic Arts (2025)
Sponsors KKR, TPG, Goldman Sachs Capital Partners (club) Silver Lake + Saudi PIF + Affinity Partners (co-invest)
Enterprise value ~$45B ~$55B
Sponsor equity ~$8B (~17–20%) ~$36B (~65%)
Debt ~$36B (24B senior secured loans syndicated; ~11B high yield via bridge) ~$20B (≈$18B funded at close), JPMorgan sole underwriter
Leverage (debt / LTM EBITDA) ~8.5x ~7.5x
Purchase multiple utility-low ~20x EBITDA
Outcome one of the largest bankruptcies ever TBD

Why tech used to be un-LBO-able, in the hosts' arithmetic: if a company costs 20x EBITDA and banks lend only 7–8x, the other 12–13 turns (60–65%) must be equity, but sponsors dislike going above ~30% equity because it dilutes returns. EA's 65% equity is that math forced through. Silver Lake's 2013 Dell buyout is the precedent they cite for tech LBOs working. - Business significance: Lenders get paid first; equity absorbs the first loss. A thin check (TXU) means a modest fall in enterprise value wipes out the sponsor and hits lenders; a fat one (EA) protects banks but makes sponsor returns hard to hit (see §4.8). Value is created by EBITDA growth, debt paydown, and multiple expansion; it is captured by whoever holds the levered slice. - Forces & impact: Credit appetite (spreads near all-time tights per the hosts), rates (Fed funds ~5.25% in 2007 vs. ~4–4.25% at recording), regulatory leverage guidance (~6x), and the multiple paid. Second-order: when purchase multiples outrun what lenders will fund, equity checks balloon and the "LBO" becomes a levered growth-equity deal. - With vs. without: Without leverage, a sponsor buying at 20x earns roughly the business's unlevered return. With TXU-style leverage, small changes in value swing equity by multiples (energy prices fell, the equity was gone). - Applies when cash flow is stable and predictable enough to service fixed claims. Breaks when cash flow is cyclical or commodity-linked (TXU: natural gas collapsed), or when the multiple paid needs growth the debt schedule can't wait for. - Channel example: LBO in Under 3 Minutes; Eerie Similarities Between Record Setting 2025 LBO (EA) and 2007 TXU LBO; Largest LBO EVER!!! Harbinger of another 2008? - Counterpoint: Kristen's heuristic that 8.5x leverage means "about 8.5 years to repay" uses EBITDA as if it were all free cash flow. After interest, tax, and capex, payback is far longer, and at TXU-era rates interest alone ate much of the EBITDA. The "under 6x" benchmark she attributes vaguely ("SEC?") is the 2013 US bank regulators' leveraged-lending guidance (Fed/OCC/FDIC), relaxed after 2018. And the PIF's motive (influence, not IRR, per the hosts) means EA's equity may accept returns a pure financial buyer wouldn't; the 65% check is partly a strategic subsidy. - Links: tiger sisters private capital 101 (LBO intro, Toys "R" Us); GLOSSARY "LBO".

4.8 Paper LBO, IRR and the rule of 72

  • What it is: A paper LBO is the mental-math version of a buyout model used in PE interviews: entry price, debt, exit price, and the resulting multiple of money (MOIC) and internal rate of return (IRR). The rule of 72 says money doubles in ~72 ÷ r years at r% a year.
  • How it works (Kristen's numbers, LBO in Under 3 Minutes):
Entry Exit (year 5)
EBITDA $1.0M $1.5M (sales up, costs cut)
Multiple 10x 10x (held flat)
Enterprise value $10M $15M
Debt $7M $6M ($1M of cumulative cash flow repaid)
Sponsor equity $3M $9M (15 − 6)

$3M → $9M is a 3.0x in five years, which she calls a 25% IRR (exactly: 3^(1/5) − 1 = 24.6%). Decompose the $6M equity gain: $5M from EBITDA growth at a constant multiple (83%) and $1M from debt paydown (17%); multiple expansion contributed nothing. Note the leverage effect: the business rose 50% in value; the equity tripled. Rule-of-72 check (this note's): a 3.0x is ~1.6 doublings; five years ÷ 1.6 ≈ 3.2 years per doubling; 72 ÷ 3.2 ≈ 23%, close to the true 24.6% (the rule understates at high rates). Shortcuts worth memorizing: 2.0x in 5 years ≈ 15%, 2.0x in 3 ≈ 26%, 3.0x in 5 ≈ 25%. Applied to the hosts' EA figures (this note's arithmetic): EV $55B at ~20x → EBITDA ≈ $2.75B; debt $20B; equity $36B. A 2.0x in five years needs exit equity $72B → EV $92B (debt held flat), so EBITDA must reach $4.6B at 20x (~11% a year) or ~$6.1B if the multiple falls to 15x (~17% a year). And leverage cuts both ways: on TXU's $8B equity / $45B EV, a 10% rise in EV is a 56% equity gain; on EA's $36B / $55B, only 15%. That is why a 65% check is a return problem: "harder to make the math work." - Business significance: IRR is how sponsors are judged and paid (carry hurdles, §4.20). Paper-LBO math lets you sanity-check a pitch instantly: a sponsor promising 25% on a 65%-equity deal must be assuming heroic growth, multiple expansion, or a dividend recap. - Forces & impact: Time is in the denominator. IRR rewards fast exits, which encourages early recaps and quick flips; MOIC rewards actual value created. Slow exit markets (the hosts' "exits are taking longer", continuation vehicles) crush IRR even when MOIC holds. - With vs. without: Without leverage, Kristen's deal is $10M → $15M, a 1.5x (~8.4% IRR). With 70% debt, the same operating result is a 3.0x. Without IRR discipline, a 2x over ten years (~7%) looks like a win; with it, that's below the long-run equity market. - Applies when cash flows are lumpy (in at entry, out at exit). Breaks when interim distributions and recycling make IRR gameable (early dividends inflate it), or when comparing deals of different durations, where MOIC and IRR disagree. - Channel example: LBO in Under 3 Minutes (the worked deal); EA/TXU figures from Eerie Similarities…. The dedicated Paper LBO and Rule of 72 shorts still have no transcript (§7). - Counterpoint: Her example ignores fees (§4.9), interest cost, and taxes, and $1M of cash flow over five years is conservative for a business earning $1–1.5M of EBITDA a year; real debt paydown would usually be larger and returns higher. The flat 10x multiple is the honest assumption; sponsors' models often quietly assume expansion. - Links: GLOSSARY "IRR"; tiger sisters private capital 101.

4.9 Sources & uses, cash-free debt-free, and rollover equity

  • What it is: The sources and uses table is the one-page budget of a buyout: where every dollar comes from (debt tranches, sponsor equity, the target's own cash) and where it goes (buying the business, refinancing its debt, fees). Cash-free, debt-free is the convention for buying a private company: the buyer pays for the business as if it had no cash and no debt; the seller keeps its cash and pays off its own debt. Rollover equity is when sellers take part of their price as equity in the new private company instead of cash.
  • How it works (Kristen, Cash Free Debt Free EXPLAINED): The house again: you buy the whole house; if the seller has a mortgage, it gets paid off at closing; a safe full of cash in the living room leaves with the seller.
  • Private target (cash-free, debt-free). Uses: purchase of the enterprise + transaction fees (bankers, lawyers) + financing fees (cost of raising the debt) + minimum cash the business needs to operate. Sources: senior debt + subordinated debt + sponsor equity.
  • Public target. Uses: buy every share, usually at a premium + refinance the existing debt + transaction and financing fees. There is no minimum-cash line: the cash comes with the shares you bought. So it shows up on the sources side as excess cash: everything on the balance sheet above what the business needs (she uses ~$10–25M as the keep-back) helps fund the deal, alongside senior debt, sub debt and sponsor equity.
  • The two framings reconcile to the same economics "99% of the time." Rollover (Skechers, Skechers' $9B deal…A Primer on Rollover Equity): 3G Capital offered shareholders either $63 cash or $57 cash + one equity unit in the private company (unlisted, untradeable). Rollover is capped at 20% of the equity so 3G owns at least 80%. Anyone electing the unit is implicitly valuing it above $6. Normally rollover is reserved for management; offering it to all holders lets those sitting on a ~20% loss (tariff uncertainty) keep upside instead of crystallizing it. Jen's analogy: selling your house to a flipper for $450k instead of $500k in exchange for a share of the $1M resale.
  • Business significance: S&U is where the equity check (§4.7) is actually computed, and fees are visible as a cost the sponsor must earn back. Rollover reduces the cash the sponsor must raise, aligns sellers with the buyer, and signals the seller's confidence; for the buyer it is cheaper equity with no fee load.
  • Forces & impact: In public-to-private deals, the premium is the price of control; excess cash on the target's balance sheet is free financing, which makes cash-rich public companies attractive targets. Going private also removes quarterly disclosure, which is the management-side reason (Skechers working through tariffs out of public view).
  • With vs. without: Without the cash-free, debt-free convention, every private deal would argue over how much the seller's cash and debt are "worth"; with it, price is set on the business and the balance sheet is settled mechanically (in practice via a working-capital adjustment at close). Without rollover, sellers must choose between full exit and no deal.
  • Applies when buying a whole business whose capital structure will be replaced. Breaks when "debt-like items" are contested (deferred revenue, unfunded pensions, accrued bonuses), which is where real-world CFDF disputes live, and for rollover when minority holders end up locked in a private company with no liquidity and no control.
  • Channel example: Cash Free Debt Free EXPLAINED; Skechers' $9B deal shows why in LBOs, cash isn't always king.
  • Counterpoint: The short treats the private-company case as the "cleanest" and skips the working-capital peg and debt-like-item fights that actually consume the negotiation. On Skechers, the hosts frame the unit as upside participation; it is also illiquid, subordinated to a large new debt load, and controlled by 3G.
  • Links: tiger sisters private capital 101 (LBO structure); §4.2 (EV: what the "uses" buy).

4.10 Who funds the debt: syndication → CLO → private credit

  • What it is: A bank that "underwrites" an LBO commits to provide the money, but traditionally it doesn't keep it. It syndicates term loans to other banks and institutional buyers (the broadly syndicated loan, BSL, market), bridges the high-yield bonds until they can be sold, and sells loan pieces into CLOs (collateralized loan obligations: pools of senior secured loans financed by tranches of debt plus an equity slice). Private credit is the alternative: one lender, holding.
  • How it works: TXU: Citi, JPMorgan, Goldman structured ~$24B of senior secured loans and syndicated them across Credit Suisse, Morgan Stanley and others; ~$11B was to be high-yield bonds, bridged by the banks. CLO managers bought loans first into a bank-financed warehouse, then the CLO priced and took the loans off bank balance sheets. Jen's analogy: a car maker stockpiling parts for orders that may be cancelled; the bank earns the markup and carry, until buyers vanish and it is left with "8,000 steering wheels" (2007–08, hung deals, fire sales). EA: JPMorgan alone committed $20B, the largest single-bank buyout underwrite ever per the hosts, backed by ~$50B of its own direct-lending capacity as a fallback if it can't syndicate.
  • Business significance: Distribution is what lets a bank lend again; Jen's point is that securitization exists so lenders don't "face" one borrower forever. Fees accrue at each handoff (underwriting, warehouse carry, CLO structuring). Private credit charges more (one lender, more customization) but offers certainty and privacy.
  • Forces & impact: Rates and spreads (floating-rate loans get cheaper as rates fall), bank capital rules, and investor demand for yield. When demand is strong, concentration feels safe; when it turns, concentrated holders are forced sellers.
  • With vs. without: Without syndication, the largest deals can't be done by any one bank, and each bank carries undiversified risk. With it, risk is spread, but in 2007 it was spread into buyers who were simultaneously exposed to mortgage CDOs, so they all disappeared at once.
  • Applies when the risk can be sold to diversified holders. Breaks when the distribution channel freezes (2007–08) or when the originator chooses to hold (EA), concentrating risk in one balance sheet.
  • Channel example: Eerie Similarities…; Largest LBO EVER!!! (Part 2 on what "underwriting" means is in the missing short Largest Debt Commitment in History for LBO by ONE BANK).
  • Counterpoint: Kristen defends CLOs hard: underlying loans are senior secured with covenants, ~70c recovery, managers often hold the equity tranche, and corporate defaults were modest even in 2008. That's largely right historically, but she concedes covenant protection has eroded (covenant-lite, incurrence-only tests, §4.12), which weakens exactly the protection she relies on. Jen's counter is the fair one: a private-credit book can't be checked from outside ("okay, you say so").
  • Links: GLOSSARY "CLO"; market structure 24 5 institutional response.

4.11 Club deals vs. co-invest

  • What it is: A club deal pools several PE firms as co-sponsors. A co-invest has one lead sponsor that runs the business while its limited partners (LPs) or strategic investors put extra equity directly into the deal alongside the fund.
  • How it works: TXU was a classic club (KKR + TPG + GSCP, $8B). EA looks like a club but the hosts read it as co-invest: Silver Lake is the operator; PIF (>$1T AUM) supplies most of the $36B; Affinity Partners (~$5B AUM, founded 2021) is the puzzle. Even a large sponsor fund (~$25B, the rough ceiling they cite) won't put $36B, or even a big fraction of its fund, into one deal. The LP gets exposure without paying 2-and-20 on that capital.
  • Business significance: Clubs blurred accountability; the hosts point to Caesars (Apollo and TPG), where sponsors fought over direction and litigation followed. Co-invest keeps one decision maker and gives big LPs cheaper exposure, which is why it displaced clubs.
  • Forces & impact: Sovereign wealth with non-financial goals (PIF's image-building, LIV Golf) is now a major equity source; its return hurdle may be lower, which lets prices rise.
  • With vs. without: Without co-invest, $50B+ buyouts require multiple sponsors and their governance friction; with it, one sponsor can do a deal several times its own appetite.
  • Applies when a trusted operator and deep-pocketed LPs coexist. Breaks when the co-investor's goals diverge (influence vs. IRR), or the lead gets preferential economics that misalign it with co-investors (the hosts speculate Silver Lake may get a sweetened structure).
  • Channel example: Eerie Similarities…
  • Counterpoint: The Affinity/PIF roles are speculation on air ("according to ChatGPT" for the AUM figure). Treat the motive analysis as opinion.
  • Links: tiger sisters wealth mechanics (club deals in family-office context).

4.12 Collateral, covenants, recovery, and the bankruptcy chapters

  • What it is: Secured lenders lend against collateral (receivables, inventory, buildings) and protect themselves with covenants: maintenance covenants are tested every quarter (e.g., leverage below X), incurrence covenants only bite when the borrower takes an action (new debt, dividends). In distress, Chapter 11 reorganizes the company so it continues; Chapter 7 liquidates it and pays lenders from the proceeds.
  • How it works: First Brands (auto parts) filed Chapter 11 on Sept 28 after failing to refinance ~$6B of maturing debt (the transcript says "$6 million" once, then "$6 billion"; billions is right). Investigators found roughly $2.3B of assets that "evaporated": receivables apparently pledged to more than one financier (invoice factoring done off the books, "hidden factoring"), plus off-balance-sheet liabilities, for ~$10–11B of total liabilities. Exposed: Jefferies' Point Bonita private-credit fund and UBS O'Connor (reportedly ~30% of one portfolio). Tricolor (subprime auto lending) went straight to Chapter 7. The same short set: Bed Bath & Beyond liquidated in bankruptcy, sold its brand to Overstock, and the renamed Overstock is now bidding $150M for The Container Store; the "company" is a brand bought at auction, not a revived business.
  • Business significance: Collateral is why a CLO model assumes ~70c on the dollar recovery for senior loans vs. ~0 for equity. But collateral is a claim on a document; if the same invoice backs three loans, two lenders hold nothing.
  • Forces & impact: In a yield-hungry market, lenders trade protections for spread (maintenance → incurrence), so problems surface later. Kristen: fraud is easy to hide when things go well and hard when they don't. Jen: private credit is "designed in a way that obfuscates stress" because a single lender can quietly renegotiate.
  • With vs. without: With maintenance covenants, a lender sees trouble at the first bad quarter and can renegotiate from strength. Without them, the first signal is a missed refinancing, when the collateral may already be gone.
  • Applies when collateral is verifiable and uniquely pledged. Breaks when receivables are double-pledged, off-balance-sheet obligations are hidden, or covenants are light enough that no one is looking.
  • Channel example: First Brands Bankruptcy, Gold at Record Highs & Banking Analyst Suing Over Sleep; How can Bed Bath & Beyond…bid $150M for The Container Store?
  • Counterpoint: Both hosts say outright they're not distressed experts. "History rhymes" with 2007 is suggestive; First Brands is so far an alleged fraud, not evidence of a systemic private credit failure. Two auto names don't make a cycle.
  • Links: trading floor mechanics (risk vs. client split); GLOSSARY "CLO".

4.13 Shorting bonds, repo haircuts, and settlement fails

  • What it is: To short a bond you borrow it (via a reverse repo with a dealer), sell it, and hope to buy it back cheaper. The dealer lends against collateral with a haircut sized to the client's creditworthiness, e.g., lend $95, $90, or $80 of bonds per $100. DV01 is the dollar change in a position per one-basis-point move in yield.
  • How it works: In Feb 2020 a small fund (the hosts call it a parody name; Black Brook) sold short $2.6B of 30-year Treasuries, "spraying the street" in clips across several dealers so none saw the full size. Jen's DV01: ~$4.2M per bp. The fund never sourced the borrow, failed to deliver, and COVID triggered a rally: 30-year yields fell from ~3.7% to ~3.2%, about 50bp. 50 × $4.2M ≈ $210M (the reported street loss was ~$250M), borne by dealers who had hedged by going short themselves and then were never delivered the bonds. "11,000-to-1": $2.6B ÷ 11,000 ≈ $240k of actual capital.
  • Business significance: Dealers make markets on trust and post-trade controls. The salesperson doesn't check a BlackRock's balance sheet per trade; onboarding, credit limits and settlement monitoring do that "behind the scenes." When those controls miss, the dealer is the one who is short.
  • Forces & impact: Electronic trading and fragmented execution make "spraying" easy and the aggregate invisible. Settlement (T+1) gives a one-day window where an unfunded sale looks normal.
  • With vs. without: With haircuts sized to credit, a client can't take more risk than its capital supports; without enforcement, leverage is whatever the counterparty forgets to check.
  • Applies when controls are applied at onboarding and settlement. Breaks when a client splits orders across dealers and no one aggregates exposure; when an exogenous shock moves the market before the fail is resolved.
  • Channel example: First Brands Bankruptcy… (the "Ferrari-loving trader" segment).
  • Counterpoint: The transcript gives the fund's size as "less than $250 million" and "$2.5 million" in different breaths; the 11,000:1 headline only works with the smaller figure. Jen also frames the story as boring incompetence; the more interesting lesson is that four or five dealers' controls each passed a trade that was only dangerous in aggregate.
  • Links: trading floor mechanics (risk controllers, middle office); market structure 24 5 trading.

4.14 Treasury auctions

  • What it is: The Treasury sells new debt on a fixed calendar through a single-price (Dutch) auction: everyone who is filled pays the same clearing yield, set by the last bid needed to fill the size.
  • How it works: Before the auction, the new bond trades when-issued (WI) as a yield spread to the current on-the-run, so the market prices the expected clearing level. Bidders: direct (needs a Treasury account), indirect (often via a bank), and dealers (the remainder). Non-competitive bids max out at $10M (retail); a competitive bidder can take up to 35% of the auction. If $25B of 10s are offered, the yield of the bid that fills the 25th billion clears the whole issue. Bids close 12:59, results just after 1pm. Clears above the WI yield → "tailed" (weak); at → "on the screws"; below → "stopped through" (strong).
  • Business significance: Auctions are scheduled supply shocks to the world's benchmark asset; a tail can trigger a sell-off, a stop-through a scramble rally. Dealers are obliged to absorb what others don't, which ties dealer balance sheets to fiscal deficits.
  • Forces & impact: Deficit size sets auction sizes; foreign and domestic demand sets the clearing yield. The paired short on mortgage rates adds the transmission: the Fed sets overnight rates, but 30-year mortgages price off the long end, which the market sets (and which QE can push down). The administration's directive for Fannie/Freddie to buy $200B of MBS is small against a ~$9T agency MBS market; Kristen calls it a signal more than a lever.
  • With vs. without: A discriminatory auction (each pays their own bid) pushes bidders to shade bids and favors insiders; the single price draws more aggressive, honest bidding.
  • Applies when the market is deep and the calendar predictable. Breaks when dealer balance sheets are constrained, so tails widen.
  • Channel example: The best explanation of Treasury auctions you'll find on the internet; Who Controls Mortgage Rates?
  • Counterpoint: The rates side is covered more deeply in the rates-macro cluster; this is the minimum a deal person needs.
  • Links: market structure 24 5 institutional response; bloomberg terminal instrumentation.

4.15 IPO pricing, the pop, lockups, and the direct listing

  • What it is: In an IPO, underwriting banks build a book of investor demand, set a price, buy the shares from the issuer and resell them. Primary shares raise money for the company; secondary shares let existing holders sell. A direct listing skips the underwritten offering: existing shares simply begin trading, priced by an opening auction.
  • How it works (Figma short): 12.5M primary + 24.5M secondary = 37M shares sold, against 585M fully diluted shares (~6% float, ignoring the greenshoe). Priced at $33 (→ $19.3B valuation). Banks aim for a ~15% first-day pop, i.e., price ~15% below expected trading value. Figma closed day one near $115: +$82/share × 37M ≈ $3B that went to the allocated buyers instead of Figma and its selling VCs (proceeds were ~$1.2B). Holders who didn't sell enjoy the markup but face a ~180-day lockup. Spotify (2018) instead did a direct listing: no new shares, secondary only; it had a public investor day anyone could watch; opening was delayed about half a day while the exchange found the clearing price. Its SVP's critique of IPOs: allocations favor bank relationships, middlemen arbitrage the price, retail is shut out.
  • Business significance: The pop is a cost of capital paid to allocated investors (largely the bank's best clients). Banks benefit both ways: fees from the issuer and goodwill from the buyers who get the cheap shares.
  • Forces & impact: Banks are paid by the issuer but repeat-play with buyers, so they lean toward underpricing. Brand-strong companies that don't need cash (Spotify) can skip them. The hosts also note the SEC review step means a government shutdown can stall the IPO pipeline.
  • With vs. without: Without the underwritten process, price discovery happens live, which works for well-known names and is risky for obscure ones; the company raises no new money in a pure direct listing.
  • Applies when there's real uncertainty about demand (bookbuilding reveals it). Breaks when demand is so lopsided that the "discount" becomes a 250% gift.
  • Channel example: Why Figma's stock price tripling the day of its IPO [is] a BAD THING; How Spotify Turned a Free Product into a $100 Billion Company.
  • Counterpoint: Figma's sellers sold ~6% of the company; the pop re-marked the other ~94% at ~3.5x overnight, which helps follow-on raises and employee equity. And Spotify's SVP is describing his own company's choice; few have copied it, which suggests the underwritten IPO solves problems (stabilization, a committed buyer base) he doesn't mention.
  • Links: sec filing intelligence (S-1 reading).

4.16 Private marks and related-party valuation

  • What it is: A private company has no market price; its "valuation" is the last price at which someone bought shares. If an interested party sets that price, the mark is only as good as the independence of the buyer.
  • How it works: X raised equity at a $33B valuation weeks before xAI bought it at the same figure in stock. Musk participated in that round and controls both companies, so he helped set the price at which one of his companies bought the other. Outside xAI shareholders bear the consequence of that exchange ratio. Same pattern in private credit: loans "marked at par" by the manager who earns fees on the NAV (Jen's "it's marked par, we say it is").
  • Business significance: Fees, carry, and fund performance are computed on marks. Citi's head of research describes the information gap: privates have no audited quarterly filings, and coverage is moving there anyway because the investable universe has "de-equitized" (fewer listed stocks, more value in a handful of megacaps and in large private unicorns).
  • Forces & impact: Longer private holding periods → more value sits at marks → more pressure to democratize access to private assets (retail products), which raises the cost of a bad mark.
  • With vs. without: With independent price setters and audits, the mark approximates a market. Without them, it can be the controlling party's number.
  • Applies when there's a real arm's-length round. Breaks when insiders lead the round or the manager marks its own book.
  • Channel example: The Truth About the $33Bn Elon Musk's xAI Paid for X; Citi's Global Head of Research…Covering Private Companies.
  • Counterpoint: The short says "who cares" if one person owns most of both. The answer is the minority holders, and they presumably priced the governance risk when they invested.
  • Links: canon akerlof market for lemons; tiger sisters private capital 101.

4.17 Sell-side research economics

  • What it is: Sell-side analysts build forecasts and ratings, and sell two things: insight to investors ("where is consensus wrong?") and access/judgment to companies. They work behind information barriers from bankers.
  • How it works (Lucy Baldwin, Citi): ~800 research staff cover ~3,500 listed equities plus rates, FX, commodities, credit (as baskets, not single names), and lately crypto and large private companies. Rule: once the bank is mandated on a transaction, its analysts stop publishing on that company. Her claim: commodity coverage is now table stakes (an LLM can produce it); value has shifted to star analysts that C-suites call. Research → banking used to be a common senior path; regulation made it harder; juniors now exit directly to PE and, in 2024–25, private credit.
  • Business significance: Research is a cost center that supports trading flow and banking relationships. Regulation (the 2003 Global Settlement in the US; MiFID II unbundling in Europe) cut the direct link between research and banking fees, which is why coverage shrank and why the survivors push into new areas.
  • Forces & impact: AI raises capacity per analyst; de-equitization shrinks the public universe; the growth of sponsors (PE/private credit owning IPO candidates) changes who research serves.
  • With vs. without: With independent research, investors get a dissenting voice on company narratives. Without the barrier, research becomes marketing for the bank's deals (the pre-2003 problem).
  • Applies when analysts can publish freely. Breaks when the bank is mandated (silence) or when coverage of private targets drifts into pre-IPO marketing.
  • Channel example: Citi's Global Head of Research…
  • Counterpoint: A head of research arguing the value of human analysts is talking her book. She dismisses the conflict in covering private IPO candidates as "easily mitigated." The pre-2003 history suggests otherwise.
  • Links: trading floor mechanics §3c (buy-side vs. sell-side research), §4 (information barriers).

4.18 Elite boutique vs. bulge bracket: two business models for selling advice

  • What it is: A bulge bracket is a universal bank (Morgan Stanley, Goldman, JPMorgan) that sells advice and lends, underwrites, trades and holds a balance sheet. An elite boutique (Greenhill, Lazard, Evercore, Centerview) sells only advice (M&A, restructuring) and has no balance sheet.
  • How it works (Scott Bok, Greenhill chairman, Elite Boutique vs. Bulge Bracket):
  • History. Charging for M&A advice is recent: Wall Street once earned its money underwriting and gave merger advice away; Bob Greenhill built Morgan Stanley's M&A department with about four people. In the 1980s–90s consolidation (Glass-Steagall erosion; the British merchant banks absorbed; tech specialists like Robertson Stephens and Alex. Brown bought) left roughly nine firms owning investment banking. Boutiques were the backlash: clients began to doubt that a bank selling them loans, bonds and hedges was purely on their side. The boutique sells conflict-free advice. Bok's mentor's image of advice inside a trading firm: the hot dog stand in front of the casino, which has a bad day whenever the traders do.
  • Risk. With no balance sheet or trading book, the firm was "our phones and our desks": the worst case is less work, not losses. Scale matters for firms holding volatile assets or deposits (he cites SVB), not for advisers.
  • Diversifying within advice. Greenhill added restructuring in 2001 as a countercyclical hedge (bankruptcy work peaks when M&A dies); most boutiques followed. Geography is the other hedge (Australia held up while Europe's banks sank after 2008).
  • Greenhill's IPO. Founded 1996, ~$100M revenue for several years; IPO in 2004 at ~100 people, ~16x oversubscribed, ~$500M value at the end of day one, ~$2B within 18 months for ~125 people. Lazard and Evercore listed in the next two years. During 2008 its stock hit an all-time high the week Lehman failed: "best house in a bad neighborhood."
  • The reversal. After 25 years many firms looked like Greenhill; Bok sold to Mizuho (2023) because inside a multi-product bank, trading does well in volatility while M&A clients freeze, which smooths the cycle. The episode gives no price (outside sources: ~$550M including debt).
  • Today. The industry has "refragmented": elite boutiques, single-industry or single-country specialists, and foreign banks (Mizuho, RBC, Nomura) building US advisory.
  • Business significance: The two models capture value differently. The bulge bracket can bundle a financing commitment with the advice (JPMorgan's $20B on EA, §4.10), which wins mandates and earns fees on several products, at the cost of conflicts and capital. The boutique earns on reputation and senior attention alone, so its pitch is independence, and its value is concentrated in a few rainmakers. For juniors: entry pay is nearly identical (§4.22: boutiques maybe ~$10k more), but the experience differs. Bok's test is to join a "Navy SEALs" unit, not a "General Motors factory," which can be a small group inside a mega-bank, and never to choose on brand or an extra $5,000 of base.
  • Forces & impact: M&A cycles hit pure advisers hardest; restructuring and geography are their only hedges. Regulation since 2008 (bank capital rules Bok calls "generals fighting the last war") raised the cost of the universal model and helped boutiques win share. The cycle can also run the other way: public boutiques face quarterly scrutiny, and the halving of US listed companies (take-privates, mergers) shrinks the client base.
  • With vs. without: Without boutiques, every major board's adviser would also want to lend to, underwrite and trade against it. With them, boards hire a boutique for the opinion and a bulge bracket for the money, which is now common on large deals.
  • Applies when a client values independence and senior attention (boards, special committees, restructurings). Breaks when the deal needs a financing commitment, or a downturn hits a firm with no other revenue.
  • Channel example: Elite Boutique vs. Bulge Bracket Investment Banks feat. Greenhill Chairman, Scott Bok.
  • Counterpoint: Bok sold his boutique into a bank, which is itself a verdict on the pure model at subscale. The episode never covers fees (retainer vs. success), deal-size bands, or analyst pay, so the title promises more comparison than it delivers. "Conflict-free" is also relative: boutiques have conflicts of their own (success fees reward getting a deal done).
  • Links: professional services leverage (partner-driven firms); trading floor mechanics (the trading side of the universal bank); canon jensen meckling agency theory (adviser incentives).

4.19 Banker and buy-side comp structure

  • What it is: Wall Street pay = base salary (fixed, bi-weekly, roughly standardized across firms and cities at junior levels) + bonus (performance-based, discretionary, and the part that grows with seniority). Senior bonuses are partly deferred and subject to clawback.
  • How it works (Buyside Hub data via High Yield Harry; hosts read averages):
Level IB base IB bonus IB total (avg / 75th pct) PE/private credit total (avg / 75th)
Analyst $111k $52k $163k / $185k $165k / $191k
Senior analyst (3rd yr) — — $202k / $217.5k $182.5k / $196k
Associate $165k $114k $280k / $328k $251k / $291k
Senior associate — — — / $430k $309k / ~$350k
VP $257k $150k $409k / $500k $423k / $485k (ex-carry)

Hosts' starting base in 2006–07: ~$55–60k. Bottom-bucket juniors may get a "donut" (zero bonus, a signal to leave without severance) or more often $15–25k. MDs: base perhaps ~$200k, total in the millions; cash comp often >$1M. Deferral: a VP's ~$500k bonus might pay one-third cash, one-third deferred cash (invested but inaccessible), one-third deferred stock vesting over 3–5 years. Unvested deferrals are forfeited on leaving, so a new employer must "buy out" the deferred balance. By ~30 that balance is large enough to make you an expensive hire, hence the "last chopper out" window. Jefferies is cited for clawback periods. EU bonus cap (How a law capping Wall Street bonuses RAISED their pay): post-crisis rules limited bonuses to 2x base (1x without shareholder approval); European banks raised bases to stay competitive, so total pay held, fixed pay rose, and a bad actor now got paid more for doing nothing, because the base is guaranteed. Jen's verdict: a rule meant to rein in risk-takers ended up guaranteeing their pay. How bonuses are set and told (Industry S1E6, S1E7, S1E3 recaps): numbers are fixed in December and paid January–March depending on the firm. Analysts start in July, so their first payout is a pro-rated stub, and they stay on a summer cycle for about two years before a stub catches them up to the winter cycle at promotion (Jen's 2008 Barclays stub was "little more than a cup of coffee"). Analyst bonuses are tiered (Kristen guesses ~five buckets), and juniors now learn the tiers through anonymous polls. Senior variable pay is a function of personal, desk, division and firm results against the desk budget; the range widens from ~$200k to $2M+ with seniority. "Don't talk about your comp" survives as policy, and the hosts call it a control tool: without comparisons you can't tell you're underpaid. Kristen calls VP pay of ~$500k "public domain." Clawbacks at banks are rare in practice: deferred pay is forfeited if you're fired for cause, kept if you resign; the realistic punishment is a donut next year. MDs may not top up juniors from their own pockets; excess pay must come from the pool. Hedge funds are different: clawbacks can be contractual (Jen's illustration: paid $80M, asked for $79M back after a down year). Guarantees when switching (Industry S2E7): a trader moving firms typically asks for a two-year guarantee; all-cash with no deferral is "not happening" today. A guarantee borrows from future pay: when it expires you are almost always "paid down," because the new bank stretched to hire you. Battlefield promotions (more responsibility without the title or pay) are why switching is often the only way to reset comp. - Business significance: Deferral aligns senior pay with multi-year outcomes and creates retention ("golden" or, for mid-levels, "silver handcuffs"). Bonus pools flex with revenue, so the bank's cost base flexes too. Desks cross-subsidize: a star on a bad-year desk is paid less, and a weak performer on a good-year desk is carried. - Forces & impact: Deal volume (2025 was "the year of the banker": IPOs and M&A back), buy-side fundraising (tight, so the sell side is more competitive than in the ZIRP years), regulation. Second-order: buy-side comp at junior levels is roughly equal to or below IB before carry, which undercuts the old "exit ASAP" logic. - With vs. without: Without deferral, a trader can take risk that pays this year and blows up next, then leave; clawbacks plus deferral make him wear the tail. Without a bonus cap, pay flexes with performance; the cap's unintended effect was guaranteed pay, the opposite of its aim. - Applies when comparing like-for-like (an MBA associate vs. a first-year big-law lawyer at ~$250–400k, per the hosts). Breaks when carry enters (§4.20) or for top-bucket outliers. - Channel example: EXACTLY How Much Investment Bankers & Private Equity Get Paid feat. High Yield Harry; Why I walked away from over $200k of my bonus at Morgan Stanley; How a law capping Wall Street bonuses RAISED their pay; Industry S1E6 "Nutcracker"…Bonus Season; Industry S1E7 "Pre Crisis Activity"…Bonus Clawbacks; Industry S2E7 "Lone Wolf and Cub"…How Investment Bankers Get Paid. - Counterpoint / dated: Survey data is self-reported. The hosts flag the VP figure as low versus their anecdotal S&T experience (+$100–200k). The UK scrapped the cap in late 2023; the EU's remains. The hosts' framing ("bonus is a misnomer, it's performance pay") is accurate but also defends their old industry from a public perception problem. In S2E7 the team-pricing arithmetic doesn't close (half of 4 × $1M is $2M, not the "$4–8M" Jen lands on). Jen's FTC non-compete point (S1E7) is dated: the 2024 ban was struck down and later abandoned. TARP is the Troubled Asset Relief Program, not "Recovery" (S1E7). - Links: canon jensen meckling agency theory; professional services leverage (fixed associate pay at law firms, the comparison case).

4.20 Carry economics by fund size

  • What it is: PE and credit funds charge "2 and 20": ~2% a year of assets as a management fee and ~20% of profits as carried interest (carry), usually after a return hurdle. Individuals get slices of the carry pool, quoted in basis points (bips) of the fund's carry, vesting over ~5 years.
  • How it works (hosts' arithmetic): A $10B fund earns $200M a year in fees; a $1B fund earns $20M. If each doubles its money, carry is $2B vs. $200M. Buyside Hub: at ~$4–5B funds, mid-levels get ~20–40bps of carry; at ~$8–10B, ~30–50bps starting at senior associate; at $200–500M lower-middle-market funds, 100–500bps (1–5%), and a junior associate may get a point or more. Megafunds (Apollo, Thoma Bravo) give associates no carry. Sub-$5B funds may add $50–500k of other equity incentives. Hours: private credit ~55–60/wk, PE ~65–70, megafund PE can match banking.
  • Business significance: 100% of zero is zero (Jen). A big carry percentage at a small fund can be worth less than a small slice at a megafund, and carry is paid years later if at all. Small funds substitute carry for cash because they can't match the fee-funded salaries.
  • Forces & impact: Exit slowdowns and continuation vehicles stretch the carry timeline; fundraising difficulty makes senior seats sticky ("top-heavy"), so juniors stall. Private credit comp has plateaued, per Harry, as seats fill with PE refugees.
  • With vs. without: Without carry, buy-side pay is IB-like or lower. With it, the payoff is a call option on fund performance, which is the real reason to move.
  • Applies when the fund performs and you stay through vesting. Breaks when the fund underperforms the hurdle, or you leave before vesting.
  • Channel example: EXACTLY How Much Investment Bankers & Private Equity Get Paid.
  • Counterpoint: Harry runs a comp-data platform; "you can go to the table on carry" is also his product's pitch. The 2x-in-a-period illustration ignores hurdles and the time value of carry.
  • Links: tiger sisters private capital 101 (2 and 20); harlem capital vc insights (European vs. American waterfalls, clawbacks to LPs).

4.21 The career pipeline: 2+2+2, on-cycle recruiting, and the MBA

  • What it is: The traditional elite path was 2 years as an IB analyst → 2 years at a PE firm → 2 years of MBA → back to PE. On-cycle recruiting is the compressed, megafund-led window in which PE firms interview first-year analysts for associate jobs starting ~18 months out.
  • How it works: In 2006–07 on-cycle came about six months into the job, after a first review. Game theory pushed it earlier ("if Apollo does it, we must"), until firms interviewed analysts before they'd started work, effectively hiring on school pedigree. JPMorgan responded by requiring new analysts to attest they wouldn't recruit elsewhere in their first months. PE firms began hiring straight from undergrad to stop paying banks' recruiting premium (banks spend heavily to train analysts), and per the hosts some are unhappy with results. Banks now try to keep analysts. The MBA as a career-switch tool: High Yield Harry calls it "LBOing yourself" (borrowing to buy an option on a better career), worth it mainly if you lack the network. The undergrad funnel (From Intern to Offer): applications for a junior-summer internship now open as early as January of sophomore year, a rolling ~16–18-month window; sophomore internships almost never convert, and the junior internship is the real 10-week interview. Offers are a ranking market: at a ~150-person bulge-bracket S&T program, interns rank desks and desks rank interns, and "if no desk ranks you first" an offer is hard to justify. Programs hire more summers than full-time seats, then attrition (firings, quits, visa failures) reopens seats for the senior-fall cycle. Offers are rarely rescinded, Jen argues, because juniors are cheap options: firms "overhire and overfire" (Lehman honored incoming offers through bankruptcy). Training then takes 2–3 months, including a two-week modeling bootcamp (Mindy Kaling reaction episode); interview technicals have inflated from "how do you value a company" (Kristen, 2007) to deferred taxes. The PE conveyor (sophomore PE, junior IB, PE offer starting two years later) selects on resumes, not observed work; Kristen on her own early hire: "on paper though, I looked great." Other doors: alumni outreach beats cold LinkedIn (Our Number One Tip); the MBA is the main reset for career switchers because associate classes have hundreds of seats built for non-finance people; sector expertise can enter via equity research. Licensing: the SIE ($80, no sponsor needed, often expected before day one), then Series 7/79/63; the CFA (three levels, ~40% average Level I pass rate, ~$1,000 registration) fits asset management and S&T better than IBD, where modeling is a footnote (CFA for Investment Banking). S&T is more a career than a two-year program: banks barely recruit S&T from MBAs, and it has become a talent farm for hedge funds, where a senior bank trader's "couple million" can become tens of millions. Trading interviews test thinking under adverse selection: a counterparty offering you a bet is itself information (Sneak peek into the interview for one of Wall Street's highest-paid jobs).
  • Business significance: IB is PE's outsourced training and screening program; on-cycle is PE free-riding on that screen. Deferral (§4.19) makes the window close around 30.
  • Forces & impact: Hours (Centerview analyst lawsuit over a sleep accommodation, not dismissed; the hosts doubt it changes practice), AI threat to junior work, and buy-side fundraising.
  • With vs. without: Without the analyst program, PE would have to train and screen itself (it's trying); without on-cycle, PE would hire on observed performance instead of pedigree.
  • Applies when buy-side seats are plentiful. Breaks when fundraising stalls, so senior seats freeze and the "+2" step vanishes.
  • Channel example: EXACTLY How Much…; Is an MBA worth it?; First Brands… (Centerview segment); Citi's Global Head of Research (research exits); From Intern to Offer: The Unwritten Rules of Wall Street Success; Our Number One Tip to Break Into Investment Banking; CFA for Investment Banking (with Kaplan's Joyce Schnur); How to Network Like a Pro feat. Jen Prosek (networking as "giving to receive": make introductions and ask nothing; judge conferences by meetings that convert within six months).
  • Counterpoint: The hosts' Centerview take ("wrong job") is the generation that survived the system judging it. They acknowledge deaths from overwork and still frame an 8-hour sleep request as 9-to-5 entitlement; reasonable people disagree. Their own suggestion (follow-the-sun global teams, AI) is the more useful idea. Kaplan's guest is selling exam prep and misstates details: CFA Level I has 180 questions, not 150; the SIE launched in 2018; the charter also needs ~4,000 hours of work experience; licenses lapse after two years out of the industry (extendable), not immediately.
  • Links: trading floor mechanics (seat comparison); professional services leverage (Cravath tournament: the same pyramid logic).

4.22 Folded in from the culture-other recaps (Industry / Succession / Strangers)

The TV recaps hold more real teaching than their titles suggest. Only the mechanisms not already covered above are listed here, compressed. Source episodes: Succession S3 Part 1 (E-wsDCA0I5I) and Part 2 (2aT4Mofm8ho); Strangers (3fbWStK44P0, I3XGEgKGDLI); Industry S3E6 (H2jaqoTmfzY), S3E8, S4 premiere, S4E4, S4E5, S4E8. Pass 2 read the second half in full: the Mindy Kaling reaction (RFFok3hycaQ), Bankers vs. Doctors (Yc25Hc4AeaY), Industry S1E3 (xYByha9veu0), S3E1 (XYoNNAlefC8), S3E7 (WaQm3U-mjwM), S4E1 (n7YeX2tgykQ), S4E2 (Rig7FMhill8), S4E6 (YXfRCC0il58), S4E7 (bywWURDpNWI), Uppity Working Women (jjH3Wtiz9EE) and the remaining culture shorts. S1E3 and Uppity Working Women are garbled machine translations (S1E3 also cuts off mid-sentence), so check their figures; Uppity Working Women and S4E2 contain almost no finance. The bulge-bracket vs. boutique teardown now has its own section (§4.18).

  • Deferred stock is a bet on your employer (Industry S3E6). Juniors are paid mostly in cash. The stock share and the deferral length both grew after 2008. Jen watched Lehman colleagues' locked-up net worth go to zero, so her rule is to take as much cash as possible if you work at a bank. That's the employee's view of §4.19: deferral aligns you with the firm, and it also concentrates your wealth in the firm.
  • Hedge fund clawbacks and crystallization (Strangers; Industry S4E8). Hedge funds claw back pay more than banks do. At pod shops (Millennium, Citadel, Point72) a PM can have one great year, blow up the next, and be clawed back and out. Performance fees usually crystallize in December, but fund documents can allow earlier payouts. Worked example on $250M AUM: 2% fee ≈ $5M, plus 20% of $110M profit = $22M, so ≈ $27M earned. "Points" (1% of firm profits) are the hedge fund version of carry.
  • Fee compression (Strangers). Their 2-and-20 example: $100M AUM pays a $2M management fee. Grow it to $150M and 20% of the $50M gain is $10M. Fund-of-funds fees fell from 1-and-10 to roughly 50bp flat once allocators did manager diligence themselves. The average hedge fund fee is ~1.67%, citing a Goldman prime-brokerage report. Long-only managers earn ~50–75bp. The fee you can charge tracks how much alpha you deliver that clients can't replicate themselves.
  • First-loss structures (Industry S4E4). The manager absorbs the first losses in exchange for a larger share of upside (a friend's fund gets ~50% of the upside). Used for market-neutral funds. This is §4.7's equity check applied to a fund: whoever takes the first loss is paid for leverage.
  • Gross leverage and the margin spiral (Industry S4E4–S4E5). Gross leverage = (|longs| + |shorts|) ÷ NAV. On a 2x short, a 7% rise in the stock costs 14% of NAV (~$35M on $250M), which wipes out a $10M first-loss tranche. The prime broker then sells other positions to meet margin. Shorting requires a located borrow, a borrow fee, restricted proceeds and extra collateral (cf. §4.13 for bonds). Their line: the market can stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent.
  • Total return swaps and Archegos (Industry S4E5). Post ~10–20% margin for 5–10x synthetic exposure: pay SOFR plus a spread, receive the stock's return. The bank holds the shares, so nothing is publicly disclosed. Archegos spread the same bet across several prime brokers, the §4.13 "spraying" problem at equity scale. A 2021 Viacom share issuance triggered margin calls. Morgan Stanley and Goldman sold first; Credit Suisse lost ~$5B. Wirecard (€1.9B of nonexistent cash, forged bank confirmations) is their template for fraud found late, cf. §4.12.
  • M&A consideration and control (Succession S3). Offer premiums run ~20–40%. Merger-arb funds buy the gap between the trading price and the offer, while long-only "real money" sells. All-stock deals need no financing, but the seller is paid in the buyer's currency. AOL/Time Warner is the warning: AOL paid in bubble-priced stock. A cash mix is capped by debt capacity: ~6–7x EBITDA even for a stable company, less for a weaker one. Termination fees compensate the counterparty for diligence and financing costs. Twitter's was ~$1B on $44B. In the proxy fight each side spent ~$100M, and the settlement took the form of board seats plus a standstill (no takeover attempt). Valuing a company from a stake: a $350M loss is 10% of a 4% stake, so the stake is $3.5B and the company ~$87.5B. Flag: the hosts call Disney/Fox an "$85B" deal; the final price was ~$71B.
  • Convertible vs. CoCo (Industry S4E4). A convertible is debt if the stock falls and equity if it rises, which protects the investor. A CoCo (contingent convertible) converts or is written off when the issuer is under stress, which protects the issuing bank's capital (Credit Suisse AT1s were wiped out). An outside investor would demand the convertible, not the CoCo.
  • Big Law vs. banking pay (Strangers). Bulge-bracket entry pay is nearly identical across firms, and elite boutiques pay perhaps ~$10k more. Law adds ~$250k of tuition and three years of lost earnings. Profits per equity partner in 2025, per the hosts: Wachtell over $12M, Kirkland ~$11M, Davis Polk ~$9.8M. Their thesis is that elite firms became "alpha providers" by finding the loopholes behind liability-management exercises, so they are now paid like risk-takers. This extends professional services leverage.
  • S&T pay runs on budgets and sales credits (Industry S1E3; short k7ZuBMq2Sl4). Salespeople are not on commission. They earn internal "sales credits" set by a grid of product × size × trade type. Desks can double the credits on trades they want done (axes), and some banks (not all: Jen's first had none, her next did) charge negative credits, e.g. when a client "showers the street." Figures: ~2,000 credits for $100M of 5-year Treasuries vs. $0.5–1M for one structured cross-asset trade. The bonus pool depends on results against the desk budget. Making $120M on a $100M budget pays well; making $60M hands rivals ammunition to take pool for their own division. Sales and trading fight every year over whether the revenue came from bringing in the risk or taking it.
  • What an axe really is, at three levels (Industry S1E3, Jen). A desk is axed when client flow leaves it with more risk than it wants or can cheaply hedge. Inventory: bonds quoted 99/101 offered at 100 to move them, like a grocer marking down bananas. Derivative risk: a 2-year swap hedges with 2-year Treasuries plus a spread, but an 8-year point has no Treasury (only 7s and 10s), so it needs a 5-7-10 butterfly; quietly offering the risk to clients is cheaper than paying spreads on three illiquid hedges. Information: traders post axes just to learn what clients are doing, which is worth paying up for. Electronic trading compresses spreads on plain products, so desks push correlation trades (e.g., a payer swaption, effectively a put on bonds, that pays only if gold and the S&P behave a certain way): conditional exposure the client buys more cheaply than the legs, with wide bid-offer because there's no liquid market. Jen's critique of Harper's "structure" (index put + gold call + builder CDS) is that the put and the CDS are the same bet at two points in the capital structure: a portfolio, not a structure.
  • Deferred pay when switching firms (Industry S3E7). The new firm usually pays a guarantee and buys out the deferred cash and stock left behind. When the old employer's stock crashes, the deferred balance shrinks and the person becomes cheaper to hire. This is the §4.19 "expensive by 30" logic run in reverse. Options in a takeover: assume they all vest; in a stock deal they convert at the exchange ratio, in a cash deal you exercise at the strike. Goldman keeps a partner tier above MD, and because part of bank pay is stock, bankers own equity from associate level "whether you want to or not."
  • IPO mechanics, the full version (Industry S3E1, "Lumi is WeWork 2.0"). Typical float is 10–20%. Price comes from bookbuilding, not a model. The target discount is ~15%, and the pop follows from oversubscription (e.g., $200 of orders for $100 of shares), because partially filled buyers then buy in the market. The greenshoe: the bank sells ~15% more than the deal size and buys shares back in the market if the price weakens, which supports trading for the first weeks. The 180-day lockup is often followed by a follow-on offering. The bank's real stake is reputation: a broken first deal costs fees on the rest of its pipeline (they cite Facebook's IPO). Lumi itself priced at 430 against an expected ~480 close, only a ~10% discount. Banks' bake-off valuations give way to research analysts' models once they're wall-crossed, and investor orders set the final price; the S3E1 funding ladder runs friends and family ($5–25k checks) → angels → VC → growth equity → IPO, with secondary anywhere from 0% to 100% of the offering.
