Wall crossing: an S&T person brought over the information barrier can be frozen in personal positions. Kristen puts Volcker's limit on banks' fund investing at ~1% of Tier 1; the rule is 3% of any one fund and 3% of Tier 1 in aggregate. Adds to §4.15.
  • Net vs. gross leverage, and EBITDA games (Industry S3E1). Net debt = debt minus cash. Lumi made its net debt look smaller by counting uncollectable receivables as cash. EBITDA isn't GAAP, so it can be massaged, as with WeWork's "community-adjusted EBITDA." LBO practice quotes gross leverage because lenders want the worst case. What counts as cash: money-market funds yes (cash equivalents are instruments under ~3 months at purchase); receivables never, since net-30 terms can stretch to 60–90 days. $100M of debt with $10M of cash ≈ $90M of debt and none. Ties to §4.2's caveat that EV is only as honest as the debt list. Kristen's power-stack aside (same episode): nuclear and coal run constantly, wind and solar when they can, and gas plants are the flexible marginal unit, so gas sets the power price, and a gas spike raises a solar generator's margin (the show has it backwards).
  • Valuation hygiene (Industry S3E7, S4E6–S4E7). Match numerator to denominator: equity value with net income / EPS, EV with sales / EBITDA / EBIT ("EV per share" doesn't exist). Banks trade on price-to-book because their balance sheets are marked to market. Equity can be worth zero, but the whole firm cannot. Accretion/dilution refers to the buyer's EPS. Stock consideration exposes the seller to the buyer's share price before closing; Netflix–Warner Bros is cited as moving to all-cash to speed the deal up (S4E7: from roughly 90% cash to all cash; reported terms were nearer 84/16). Disclosure thresholds: 5% in the US, 3% in the UK. Porsche/VW 2008 combined ~42% of the shares with 31.5% in cash-settled options; the counterparty banks delta-hedged by buying real shares, each just under 3%, and "cash-settled" could be switched to physical by agreement. Synthetic positions carry no vote or dividend but leave a paper trail (collateral, ISDAs, confirmations), which is how a fake stake gets exposed. A bid turns hostile only after the board rejects it and the bidder goes to shareholders (bear-hug letter). The house version of equity-vs-firm (S4E6): $1M house, $800k mortgage, $200k equity; sell at $750k and the equity is zero while lenders still recover most of their money. Hence Kristen's sum-of-the-parts correction: a £12/share base case built on £2–3B of legitimate EV stays £12 when the fake acquisitions are valued at zero; it doesn't fall to zero.
  • Bank capital stacks (Industry S3E7, S4E6). Preferred equity has no principal to repay and is subordinated. TARP and Buffett's Goldman investment were structured this way, hence the hosts' "a capital injection, not a bailout." In 2008 MUFG put $9B into Morgan Stanley, mostly convertible preferred with a 10% dividend and a ~$31.25 conversion price, for 21%. Basel III minimums: 4.5% CET1, 6% Tier 1, 8% total capital; big banks run 10–14%. The show repeatedly confuses four instruments: putable bonds (investor's trigger), callable bonds (issuer's option), convertibles and CoCos.
  • 2008 plumbing and rescues (Industry S3E7). Pre-2008 swaps were bilateral under a CSA (Credit Support Annex; Jen calls it a "collateral services agreement"). If Lehman owed MS $10M and failed, MS lost the $10M and its offsetting hedge was suddenly unhedged, so losses chained bank to bank; that is why most derivatives are now centrally cleared. Lehman's 2008 was a run on liquidity (clearing banks and repo counterparties demanding collateral), not deposits, after ~$10B of capital raises (a $4B convertible preferred in April, $6B after a $2.8B Q2 loss) failed to restore confidence. Barclays bought the US business for its IBD/ECM and the 745 Seventh Ave building, not its FICC, so FICC staff were cut and everyone reinterviewed for their own jobs. The 2008 short-sale ban covered all shorting of financials, which blew up convertible-arb funds that hedge by shorting stock. Morgan Stanley stayed independent on CIC's $5B mandatory convertible (Dec 2007) plus MUFG's $9B. Kristen's TARP case: three programs, below-market preferred dividends, and MS/GS forced to take it for system confidence; TARP is often confused with QE, which is what actually drove 2009–10 bank profits. SVB (Treasuries marked down as rates rose) and Credit Suisse (a 2022 Saudi/QIA raise, then a refusal of more support, then a forced weekend sale to UBS with AT1s wiped) are her modern rhymes. Distress is defined as inability to refinance, not a falling share price. Flags: the TARP disbursed figure is ~$443B (authority cut from $700B to $475B), not her "60%" or "50% untouched"; the equity-method threshold is 20%, not 21%.
  • Liquidity matching and gating (Industry S4E1). PE locks capital up 5–7 years to match illiquid assets; hedge funds offer monthly or quarterly liquidity (multi-manager platforms lock up 3+ years). Redemptions force fire sales that can kill a fund whose thesis is right. Gating suspends outflows so stayers aren't hurt by forced selling, and it wrecks future fundraising. Allocators on the Yale model buy market beta cheaply and use hedge funds for uncorrelated absolute return, so a short-only fund is a hedge, not a market-beater; an SMA runs the client's constraints while a fund pools capital behind the manager's view. Shorting stock: locate a borrow through prime brokerage, pay the borrow fee plus any dividends owed to the lender; illiquid mid-caps are expensive to borrow. Cover in small clips across dealers so you don't squeeze yourself (S4E7). Ties to the private-credit gating discussion in wss credit distressed.
  • Fraud patterns and audit (Industry S4E6). Kristen's taxonomy. Enron (~$70B peak cap): booked a 10–15-year contract's full value on day one, hid debt and losses in SPEs, round-tripped trades to inflate revenue; Arthur Andersen died with it, and Sarbanes-Oxley (2002) created the PCAOB, CEO/CFO certification and auditor-independence rules. Valeant: R&D ~3% of sales vs. a 15–20% industry norm; bought drugs and raised prices (one +525%, another +2,700%); channel stuffing through Philidor; Ackman lost ~$4B. Luckin: simply fabricated sales, caught by store-traffic video and receipts. Lesson: complexity is cover; "the cash flow statement tells the truth." A legitimate SPV for contrast: Meta's Hyperion data center, owned and controlled by Blue Owl with Meta holding ~20% and leasing it, which keeps the debt off Meta's balance sheet. Audit outcomes: clean, qualified, adverse (and disclaimer, which she omits). Flags: Luckin's video evidence was ~11,000 hours, not "92,000"; Liberation Day was April 2, 2025, not April 9.
  • Bankruptcy waterfall and UK regulators (Industry S4E7). Senior secured → senior unsecured → subordinated → equity; Kristen's training firm recovered ~12c on the dollar on unpaid Lehman invoices, trickling in over ~10 years (the unsecured-creditor reality behind §4.12's ~70c secured figure). Bank M&A priced at ~1.2x book with a 90-day clawback works like an earn-out. UK map: the SFO prosecutes fraud (LIBOR), the FCA is roughly SEC plus CFPB, the PRA licenses banks, and a Section 166 "skilled person review" lets the regulator compel an outside firm to review governance and controls.
  • Insurance as tail-risk pricing (shorts). A-Rod's 2001 10-year, $252M contract was spread across 17 insurers; nobody would cover the last three years (performance falls after ~34), so Buffett did: the back-end years carry the risk, and the premium is the price of a tail. War-risk marine cover is priced per transit at roughly 0.25–0.30% of hull value (~$250–300k on a $100M ship), lower with armed guards, and insurers can simply withdraw cover.
  • Sell company stock when it vests (Industry S4E7). Your salary already makes you long your employer, so holding its stock as well doubles the risk. This is blanket advice; the hosts don't mention taxes. Taylor Swift masters (short): Scooter Braun bought for ~$140M and sold 17 months later for $300M. Shamrock held from 2020 to 2025, putting in $300M and selling for $360M while collecting ~$30M a year of income, about 12% a year before financing.
  • Doctors vs. bankers (Yc25Hc4AeaY). No lifetime-earnings model, but the shape is clear: residents earn ~$50–60k (NYC is now nearer $70–90k), a general pediatrician posting paid $125k, and "real money" arrives around 31–32. NYC academic medicine pays around the national median, a prestige discount. Pediatric emergency medicine pays in the low-to-mid $200ks, $50–100k less than adult EM despite more training, because insurers set pediatric reimbursement lower decades ago; incentives follow reimbursement, so cash-pay, 9-to-5 specialties (sleep, allergy) are now the competitive ones. A few surgical services subsidize the rest of the hospital. Insurers can pay up to a year late, claw back, or downcode (one paid ~$200 for a breast reduction that includes three months of post-op care), which pushes surgeons to cash pay, collected before surgery. Surgery is compared to project-based IBD and the ER to reactive S&T. Flag: $80k a year of college is $320k over four years, not the "$240k" said. Household math (short): $1M a year in NYC with three kids leaves ~$100–200k after ~$350k federal plus ~$100k state, city and payroll tax, $25–40k of health premiums, ~$200k of housing on a $2.5M apartment, and $40–72k per child of preschool plus a nanny.
  • Bankers vs. lawyers (4K9ZjBkSTT4, with a Wachtell M&A partner and a Davis Polk capital-markets partner). M&A law covers control transactions; capital markets covers raising money without selling control, and is collegial because issuer and underwriter want the same outcome, while M&A risk allocation is zero-sum. Bankers set price and consideration; lawyers set structure (direct vs. reverse triangular merger), shareholder-vote consequences, termination and reverse termination fees, and antitrust efforts covenants. Big Law first-years earn ~$225k base with a small bonus (pay weighted to base, consistent with more risk-averse people); banking pays a lower base and larger bonus, with MDs at $1–5M. Partnership takes ~8–10 years by qualitative vote, and partners buy in with capital. Most contracts are never re-read; the ones that are (a buyer trying to walk) are why the best drafters are hired up front. Flag: the vote trigger he simplifies as the cash/stock mix is really the exchange rule on issuing ≥20% of the acquirer's shares.
  • Sports franchises as assets (0Un7W_aL1H4, Eli Manning and David Adelman; routed to this cluster). Valuation tracks how much revenue is shared nationally. NFL: a ~$110B, 11-year national TV deal split equally across 32 teams plus a hard cap, so big- and small-market teams converge in value. NBA: ~60/40 national/local with a soft cap, a luxury tax and two "aprons" that add penalties and roster limits. MLB: mostly local revenue and no cap, so value depends on market and only a handful of teams make real money. The NFL now admits an approved list of PE funds (Arctos, Ares, Sixth Street, a Blackstone/Carlyle consortium) for minority stakes, which pushed money down into smaller sports assets. Adelman's point: owning the arena captures building revenue and the fan experience (the 76ers' 50/50 arena with Comcast, ~$1.5B, opening 2031), and the surrounding real estate counts toward team value. Flags: $110B/11/32 is ~$312M a team a year from TV alone, not "$400M"; Kristen's 4.2x apron "fine" is invented (the tax is tiered ~1.5–4.75x on the overage); the NBA deal is ~$76B over 11 years; Packers shares carry no economic rights, so "publicly traded" is wrong.
  • One-sidedness flags (culture-other). The two Strangers episodes contradict each other on AUM, fee terms and roles. Their claim that a short over 5% becomes public is wrong: 13D/G covers long positions, and EU/UK net-short disclosure starts at 0.1–0.5%. Their "~57% NY marginal tax" is high; the top combined federal/state/city rate is ~52%. Jen's "TARP wasn't technically a bailout" is opinion stated as fact.

5 · How the concepts connect

 three statements (§4.1) ──► unlevered FCF ──► DCF (§4.3) ──► ENTERPRISE VALUE (§4.2) ◄── comps / precedents
                                                  ▲
               WACC (§4.4): rf + β × MRP for equity; YTM × (1 − t) for debt
                                                  ▲
         tax shield, capped at 30% of EBIT(DA) (§4.6) ──► capital structure (§4.5): debt cheap until distress
                                                  │
 purchase multiple ──► debt capacity (turns of EBITDA) ──► EQUITY CHECK (§4.7) ──► sources & uses (§4.9)
                                                  │                   │
         who holds the debt: syndicate → CLO → private credit (§4.10)  ▼
                    │                                     paper LBO: IRR / MOIC (§4.8)
       covenants, collateral, recovery (§4.12)                        │
       yield-hungry market → covenant-lite → fraud found late         ▼
                                                     carry (§4.20) ──► comp: base, bonus, deferral (§4.19)
 exit: IPO (pop = transfer, §4.15) / sale / continuation;                  │
 private marks (§4.16) bridge the years with no price                       ▼
                                          who sells the advice: boutique vs. bulge bracket (§4.18)
                                          and who climbs the ladder: career pipeline (§4.21)

The causal spine: the three statements produce the cash flows; the WACC prices them, and the tax treatment of debt bends the WACC; the price paid and debt capacity set the equity check; the equity check decides both the return and who eats the first loss; the holder of the debt decides where that loss lands; and the return decides carry, which is what the whole career ladder is climbing toward. Two recurring tensions run across the chain. First, every "mechanical" step hides a judgment the seat shapes: the sell side standardizes beta and the MRP to survive a lawsuit, the buy side uses judgment, and an Industry banker lowers the WACC to please a client. Second, controls at every link (covenants, haircuts, research barriers, central clearing, deferral, clawbacks) each exist because a past failure at that link was expensive: TXU and hung bridges, Lehman's bilateral swaps, the pre-2003 research scandals, the 2008 bonus-for-blowup problem.

6 · Retrieval questions

  1. A headline says Company A was "sold for $20B less" than two years ago. What two numbers do you ask for before believing it? — Debt (and cash) at both dates. The price of the business is EV; an equity-value drop can be pure added leverage (X/xAI: 33+12 ≈ 44+0.6).
  2. Why does Kristen put the cash flow statement in the middle of a three-statement model, and why can a DCF skip the balance sheet? — It follows one dollar: net income opens the CFS, which ends in the change in cash that lands on the balance sheet. A DCF needs only unlevered cash flows (EBITDA, D&A, capex, ΔNWC), not debt or a balancing balance sheet.
  3. A company's 2020 bonds carry a 3% coupon but yield 7% today; the tax rate is 25%. What is its cost of debt for the WACC, and why not 3%? — 7% × 0.75 = 5.25%. The WACC needs today's marginal cost of borrowing; the coupon reflects 2020 rates.
  4. A sell-side banker and a buy-side investor value the same company. Why might they choose different betas? — The banker may defend a fairness opinion in court, so uses a standard (Bloomberg adjusted beta, ⅔ raw + ⅓ × 1); the investor can weigh R², use peer asset betas relevered, or a forward beta.
  5. A viewer says cost of equity is 5% because the stock trades at 20x earnings. What is right and wrong about that? — 1/PE is the earnings yield, useful for EPS accretion (stock at 5% vs. debt at 5.25% after tax), but it ignores growth and payout and is not a required return. Equity is junior to debt (loan recoveries ~76%, equity often zero), so it must cost more.
  6. Under Modigliani–Miller with taxes, adding debt raises firm value. Where does the value come from, per Kristen? — From taxpayers, through the interest deduction; it's a transfer, not created value. Bankruptcy and issuance costs (IPO fees 6–7% vs. bond fees 12–40bp) are what MM leaves out.
  7. In Kristen's LBO ($10M at 10x, $3M equity, EBITDA $1M → $1.5M, $1M of debt repaid), how much of the equity gain came from operations vs. debt paydown, and what would the unlevered return be? — $5M of the $6M gain from EBITDA growth, $1M from paydown; 3.0x ≈ 25% IRR levered vs. 1.5x ≈ 8% unlevered.
  8. Why could PE not LBO most tech companies in 2007, in one sentence of arithmetic? — At ~20x EBITDA with lenders funding 7–8x, equity must fill 60–65%, far above the ~30% that makes LBO returns work.
  9. In a public-to-private LBO, why is there no "minimum cash" line in uses, and where does the target's cash go? — Buying the shares buys the cash; excess cash above the operating keep-back appears as a source funding the deal. In a private cash-free/debt-free deal, the seller keeps its cash and repays its debt.
  10. Skechers holders could take $63 cash or $57 + one private unit. What are electors betting, and what are they giving up? — That the unit is worth more than $6 after 3G's turnaround; they give up liquidity, control and seniority (the unit sits under the new debt), within a 20% rollover cap.
  11. Why did JPMorgan's sole $20B commitment worry Jen more than TXU's syndicate did? — Distribution spreads risk; a single holder concentrates it on one systemically important balance sheet.
  12. Why does a boutique add restructuring, and why did Greenhill still sell to Mizuho? — Restructuring peaks when M&A dies, the only hedge an advice-only firm has; inside a universal bank, trading's volatility profits offset M&A droughts, and the boutique model had been widely copied.
  13. Why did the EU bonus cap increase guaranteed pay, and what does a two-year switching guarantee do to pay in year three? — Banks raised bases to hold total comp, so less pay was at risk. Guarantees borrow from the future: after they expire you are usually "paid down."
  14. How did Lehman's failure hurt Morgan Stanley even on a swap where MS was owed money? — MS lost the receivable and its offsetting hedge with another party was suddenly unhedged; bilateral exposure chained losses across banks, which is why most swaps are now centrally cleared.
